content: The Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI) guidelines are designed for outpatient care of sick children and are intended for use by doctors, senior nurses, and other experienced health professionals responsible for managing young children at the first referral level in developing countries. The first edition of the Pocket Book was reviewed by a WHO guidelines steering committee, which identified chapters requiring updates. These updates included aligning the Pocket Book with recently published WHO-approved guidelines and incorporating new evidence that had been analyzed and synthesized. The updates were categorized into two groups. The first group involved incorporating recommendations approved by the WHO Guidelines Review Committee. The second group required synthesizing evidence and making updates consistent with new recommendations. The changes made were based on WHO guidelines and recommendations published as of 2012, with additional subsections added, removed, or reorganized based on user feedback. Editorial changes were also made to improve clarity and usability. The second edition retained a similar presentation to the first edition due to its popularity and user feedback. All changes were reviewed by external clinical experts and approved by the WHO Guidelines Review Committee. A web version of the Pocket Book will be updated regularly as new clinical evidence emerges, while printed editions will be published every five years if substantial changes are required. The main changes in the second edition include updates to specific chapters. Chapters such as Triage and Emergency Conditions, Diagnostic Approaches to the Sick Child, Diarrhea, Common Surgical Problems, Monitoring the Child’s Progress, and Counseling and Discharge from Hospital underwent only editorial changes or reorganization without major updates to the content. However, chapters like Problems of the Neonate and Young Infant, Cough or Difficulty in Breathing, Fever, Severe Acute Malnutrition, Children with HIV/AIDS, and Prevention of Mother-to-Child HIV Transmission and Infant Feeding were substantially revised or restructured to reflect updated clinical guidance. The Pocket Book is designed to be portable and accessible for healthcare workers during their daily practice, providing guidance for managing sick children. While new topics have been added, standard pediatric textbooks should still be consulted for rare conditions not covered in the Pocket Book. These guidelines are applicable globally and can be adapted by countries to suit their specific needs. WHO encourages local adaptation of the Pocket Book to include important conditions not covered and believes its widespread adoption will improve hospital care for children and reduce case fatality rates. The triage process outlined in the Pocket Book emphasizes the rapid screening of sick children upon arrival at the hospital to identify those with emergency signs requiring immediate treatment, those with priority signs needing expedited assessment, and non-urgent cases. Emergency signs include obstructed or absent breathing, severe respiratory distress, central cyanosis, signs of shock, coma, convulsions, and severe dehydration in children with diarrhea. Children with these signs require immediate emergency treatment to prevent death. Priority signs identify children at higher risk of dying and should be assessed without unnecessary delay. If a child has one or more emergency signs, priority signs do not need to be checked. The steps in emergency triage assessment and treatment include checking for airway or breathing problems, assessing for shock or severe dehydration, and determining if the child is unconscious or convulsing. Emergency treatment should be initiated immediately, including airway management, oxygen administration, IV fluid resuscitation, and glucose or anticonvulsant administration as needed. Healthcare professionals are advised to remain calm, work collaboratively, and involve experienced colleagues when managing very sick children, as multiple treatments may be required simultaneously. Emergency investigations, such as blood glucose, blood smear, and hemoglobin levels, should be conducted promptly. After providing emergency treatment, the underlying problem should be assessed, diagnosed, and treated. Differential diagnoses for emergency signs are provided in the Pocket Book for further guidance. The WHO acknowledges the contributions of numerous experts, institutions, and organizations in updating the Pocket Book. Financial support for the second edition was provided by the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation and the Russian Federation. The Pocket Book aims to serve as a practical tool for improving the care of sick children in hospitals worldwide.
